Bi nou rankont ozordi se pour ogmant zot konesans e osi ganny zot kontribisyon lo diferan size ki annan pou fer avek sa lenstitisyon. Rol prensipal Labank Santral se pour promouvwar stabilite dan bann pri lo marse domestik. I osi annan lezot rol ki enkli asire ki pei i annan en sistenm finansyel ki fonksyonn byen. Avek sa an tet, tenm kin ganny swazir pou nou diskisyon ozordi se: Rol Labank Santral Sesel dan Sistenm Banker e Finansyel, e son Lenpak lo bann Endividi. Noun swazir sa tenm avek lentansyon pour anmenn Labank Santral pli pros avek piblik e ogmant zot konnenans lo nou lenstitisyon. Noun osi konstate ki nou bezwen met plis lanfaz lo sansibilizasyon e ledikasyon finansyel, si nou anvi ki piblik i pli byen konpran bann polisi ki gid nou bann aksyon e desizyon. Nou swete ki bann topik ki pou ganny aborde ozordi apremidi i ava adres serten zot bann konsern. Pour note ki serten sa bann konsern ti ganny idantifye okour enteraksyon ki bann zofisye Labank Santral in annan avek bann Digwa, pandan en vizit travay isi resaman. Noun osi pran an kont sizesyon fer dan bann rankont oparavan, e nou la ozordi avek reprezantan sorti kot Lasosyason bann Labank Sesel pou reponn zot kestyon e eklersi zot bann dout. Fason ki Labank Santral i ede mentenir stabilite dan pri lo marse domestik, son rol dan kad zefor pou protez konsomater bann prodwi e servis finansyel e modernizasyon bann sistenm peyman i parmi plizyer topik ki pou ganny aborde. Lo size mentenir stabilite dan pri lo marse domestik, depi Zilyet 2017, Labank Santral pe met plis lenportans lo amelyorasyon transmisyon lentere avek bi aforsi lefikasite polisi moneter. Asire ki lenflasyon i reste lo en nivo akseptab i vin avek son prop defi, anvi devlopman lo nivo global ki Labank Santral pa kapab enfliyanse, me ki annan lefe direk lo pri lo marse domestik. Anplis, nou pe kontinyen vwar logmantasyon dan demann pour kredi ki pa neseserman vize ver lenvestisman. Prenan kont sa bann devlopman, Labank Santral i reste vizilan e kan i neseser aziste son polisi moneter pou mentenir stabilite dan pri. Nou pou osi koz lo kimanyer zot kapab envestir dan bann lenstriman finansyel ki ganny servi par Gouvernman - sa ki nou konn konman Treasury Bills ek Treasury Bonds. Prosesis administrativ i ganny fer par Labank Santral, e sa bann lenstriman i kapab ede avek polisi moneter e ofer en loportinite seving pour manm piblik. Lafason ki nou fer peyman pour osi ganny aborde. Tradisyonnelman, nou kontan annan nou larzan dan nou lanmen letan nou fer bann tranzaksyon, ki swa pour aste en prodwi oubyen pour ganny peye pour nou servis. Sepandan, Labank Santral pe kontinyen met zefor pour enplimant plizyer linisyativ pour moderniz sistenm peyman, ki viz sirtou ver peyman an form elektronik ki vit e efikas. An 2013 par egzanp, Labank Santral an kolaborasyon avek bann labank komersyal e Seychelles Credit Union ti lans en sistenm peyman elektronik ouswa SEFT, parey dimoun i pli familye avek. Sa platform peyman sekirize i fasilit transfer larzan ant bann labank e in resaman ganny amelyore. Pareyman, an 2012, Labank Santral avek bann lenstitisyon banker ti konmans servi en sistenm elektronik pour cheques kin elimin bezwen pour fizikman transport e esanz cheques. Sa i permet kliyan pou ganny akse avek zot larzan pli vit. Modernizasyon sistenm peyman i en proze ki pou kontinyen dan sa bann lannen ki vini. Nou pour osi abord size akse avek kredi, ouswa ln, pli partikilyerman eksplik sistenm ki ranmas lenformasyon lo lafason ki kliyan i repey zot fasilite kredi ouswa Credit Information System. Sa sistenm ti ganny etabli an 2012 pour permet bann labank ganny akse avek lenformasyon pour ki zot kapab fer pli bon desizyon an fas en laplikasyon - lo si pou donn en ln oubyen non e lentere ki pou ganny sarze. Travay in konmanse pour amelyor sa sistenm e pou edik e sansibiliz piblik lo son benefis. Sa i an linny avek zefor pou asire ki bann linisyativ ki Labank Santral pe antreprann oubyen pe anvizaze, i osi pran kont drwa konsomater bann servis dan sekter banker e sekter finansyel. Dan en pti moman nou pou demar nou seri prezantasyon, e apre sa zot a ganny sans demann zot kestyon. Mon ti a kontan sezi sa loportinite pour remersi zot tou kin reponn lapel Labank Santral e ki la prezan ozordi apremidi. Mon swet zot en bon partisipasyon. Mersi pour zot latansyon.

Title: Welcoming Remarks - CBS Board-Management Retreat 2020
text: Welcoming Remarks by Ms Caroline Abel Governor of the Central Bank of Seychelles Regional Workshop Risk-Based Supervision for Digital Financial Services, Money Value Transfer Services, Money Remittances and Bureau de Change Sectors Monday 27 May 2019 Venue: Savoy Resort and Spa Secretary of State for Finance, Trade, Investment and Economic Planning Mr Patrick Payet, Representatives of the ESAAMLG Secretariat, Distinguished speakers and participants, Ladies and Gentleman, Good Morning. I am pleased to address you as we embark on this regional workshop, which the Central Bank of Seychelles is hosting, in collaboration with the Eastern and Southern Africa Anti Money Laundering Group (ESAAMLG). Let me start by extending a warm welcome to our distinguished speakers and participants from the region, who have travelled to Seychelles for this event, where 1 discussions will be centred on a subject that is of much relevance and importance to all of us. There is no doubt that the global financial landscape is evolving at an incredibly fast pace. While this brings an array of possibilities to facilitate the delivery of financial services, developments in the financial sector are also pushing the competent authorities to re-evaluate their supervisory approach. Much of the focus is on the shift towards a more risk-based approach when it comes to supervision of the various financial services, from banks to non-banks, in response to the emerging challenges and risks. This seeks to address the constraint of limited resources faced by supervisory and regulatory entities and the need for these resources to be utilised most efficiently, with particular focus on sectors or activities that pose a higher risk. For this workshop, particular attention will be paid to Risk-Based Supervision for Digital Financial Services, Money or Value Transfer Services, Money Remittances and Bureau de Change Sectors. From a local perspective, in 2016 the CBS commissioned a study to assess the remittances market and highlight the importance of remittance flows to and from Seychelles. Data covering a 9 month period from July 2015 to March 2016, showed that the total value of inward transfers including trade flows, employee salaries and workers remittances amounted to nearly 65 million dollars. The value of outward transfers, the majority of which were bank transfers processed through SWIFT reached almost 100 million dollars. This was the first such study to be conducted locally. According to the provisional Balance of Payments 2018, the total inward 2 transfers amounted to 104 million dollars and Outward transfers 160 million dollars, of which the estimated inward workers remittances is 26 million dollars and the estimated outward workers remittances is 72 million dollars. According to the World Banks latest Migration and Development Brief, released in April this year, remittances to low-and-middle-income countries reached a record high in 2018 at the tone of 529 billion US dollars. This represents an increase of 9.6 per cent over the previous record high documented in 2017. On a global scale, remittances, which include flows to high-income countries, reached 689 billion dollars in 2018, while in the region, remittances to Sub-Saharan Africa is said to have grown almost 10 per cent in 2018. It is expected that remittance flows to low-and-middle-income countries will reach 550 billion dollars in 2019, becoming their largest source of external financing. From these figures, it is evident that money remittance services including digitally enabled cross-border remittances are not only facilitating the delivery of financial services, but also helping to drive down costs and enhance financial inclusion. However, it is essential to note that in spite of their capabilities to help foster enabling environments, such services are raising key policy and regulatory challenges for regulators, such as their vulnerability to abuse, in particular money laundering and terrorist financing risks. Hence, supervision of this sector and the ability of the authorities to take effective and proportionate enforcement actions in cases of anti-money laundering and counter financing of terrorism breaches is of utmost importance. 3 It is for this reason that supervising entities are under much pressure to move away from a one-size fits all approach to supervision and risk assessments, particularly the traditional rules-based approach, and to adopt smarter policies to improve oversight of their reporting entities. Risk-based supervision calls for supervisors to strategically allocate and use their resources although sometimes scarce, as well as prioritise and adjust interventions according to identified and adequately-assessed risks. Much emphasis is also placed on ensuring that any Risk-Based Framework should be forward-looking to allow for timely interventions, to address not only the present but also future risks and challenges. I am mindful that we all have our constraints in this regard, due to the unavailability of high-quality data and limited resources, including human capacity, as well as legal challenges. One of the objectives of the workshop is essentially geared towards assisting the participating countries in building the capacity of their supervisory or regulatory authorities to carry out more targeted risk assessments and develop appropriate risk- based supervisory frameworks. Capacity building, improvement in knowledge sharing, and increased use of technology solutions to improve on regulatory compliance and financial supervision, are some of the critical areas to focus on, as we invest time and resources to implement a Risk-Based approach to supervision. 4 For Seychelles, this was already one of the recommendations highlighted in the second Mutual Evaluation Report adopted in September last year. Work has already started in that respect, and much of the initiatives are being coordinated by the National Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) Committee set up earlier this year. The Committee has representation at the highest level from relevant institutions, namely the Finance Ministry, Attorney Generals Office, Police, Anti-Corruption Commission, Financial Services Authority, Financial Intelligence Unit, Registration Division, Seychelles Revenue Commission and Central Bank itself, all of which are being represented at this workshop. While the development of a Risk-Based Supervision model for prudential supervision is underway, there is also a need to develop the Risk-Based Framework from an AML perspective. This will be primarily guided by amendments to legislation including the Anti-Money Laundering Act, which will make provision for sectoral supervision for AML/CFT purposes. These amendments will allow for each supervisory authority to implement a Risk-Based Supervision Framework for adequate monitoring of the entities and financial systems that fall under their purview. Ladies and Gentlemen, The risk-based approach is central to the implementation of the revised International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), adopted in 2012. 5 It is my strong desire to see this four-day undertaking result in equipping all of the supervisory entities gathered here, both locally and from the region, with knowledge and expertise necessary for them to design and implement risk-based supervisory frameworks in the context of digital financial services, money or value transfer services, money remittances and bureau de changes sectors. As we are very much aware, criminals are trying to find ways and means to beat the intelligence sharing and mechanisms in place to conduct their illicit transactions; such as money laundering and terrorist financing, illegal wildlife trade, cybercrime targeting new technologies, among others This is not only a cross-sectoral dilemma for our respective territories but also a cross-border issue. The broad outline of discussion topics is expected to allow you, dear participants, to share expertise, think outside the box and be more forward-looking on how we can improve risk-based supervision, not only for the benefit of our respective jurisdictions but also as a region. So let us maximise the opportunity being given through the interactions that will take place during this workshop. Let me conclude by wishing all the foreign participants and speakers a pleasant stay in Seychelles and very fruitful engagement and learning experience together with the local participants. Thank you for your attention. 6

Title: Message - International Human Band Allocation
text: Welcoming Remarks by Ms Caroline Abel Governor of the Central Bank of Seychelles CBS Board and Management Retreat Sunday 16 February 2020 Venue : Avani Seychelles Barbarons Resort & Spa Mr Mohammed Nyaoga, Chairman of the Central Bank of Kenya Board of Directors, Fellow Board Directors, Members of Management, CBS Colleagues, Good morning. Thank you for joining us here today on the second day of our Board and Management Retreat, where we will once again devote ourselves to the task of assessing our progress towards achieving our vision of becoming a Central Bank delivering price stability and financial system soundness. For the majority of us who were present yesterday, I believe you will agree with me that Day 1 provided thought-provoking sessions from which they have given us much to consider as we move forward as an institution. We started off with a stock-taking exercise of the first year of our five-year strategic cycle, noting what has worked, the challenges that are impeding our progress and what we need to do to re-adjust our strategic journey. The importance of self-care and self-worth was highlighted and we gathered tips to enable us to strike a better work/life balance. We discussed the importance of recognition and appreciation of staff performance and initiated a powerful conversation about empowering our staff, which is key in ensuring that we have the next generation of resilient central bankers but also in our current state of business how to we become more efficient by delegating more as we recognise that we already have the right competencies on the ground to do so. We also discussed on forward-looking ideas on how to recalibrate our capacity development programs which will respond to the emerging needs of central banking and the wider economy as a whole as we are mindful that our staff can become leaders externally. The line of discussion from yesterday will be further expanded today as the conversation switches to the promotion of a culture of good governance. At this juncture, I would like to acknowledge the presence and extend a warm welcome to our honoured guest, Mr Nyaoga, Chairman of the Central Bank of Kenya Board of Directors, who has graciously accepted our invitation to engage with us as we conduct a health check of the governance structure of our institution and to share insights based on his years of experience in the central banking environment. Todays programme is one that promises rich debates on our governance structure, the way we brand ourselves and the topic of wealth creation and 2 distribution has been incorporated to set the scene for our deliberations of the day. I invite you all to participate fully, without reservation, so that we can contribute to rich discussions that will produce tangible outcomes and enable us to develop a culture of inclusive growth firstly within the Central Bank, which will eventually be transmitted to the society at large through our policies and our outreach activities. On this note, I will conclude the formal part of the days programme so that we can devote our time to the substance of todays session. I look forward to our fruitful deliberations. Thank you. 3

Title: Welcoming Remarks - Capacity Building for Website Developers on Embedding Payment Gateways onto Websites
text: Launching of the Financial Literacy Baseline Survey results Opening remarks by the Governor of the Central Bank of Seychelles Time: 8:35 a.m. Venue: STC Conference Room, Victoria Minister Jean-Paul Adam, Minister Wallace Cosgrow, Invited Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen. Good morning and welcome to the presentation of the financial literacy baseline survey results. A special welcome to Mr Abel Motsomi who will be our main presenter for the day. May I begin these opening remarks with a few words on the background of this work: As part of the deliverables of the Seychelles Financial Sector Development Implementation Plan which was approved by the Government in November 2014, it was recommended that a baseline study on financial literacy be developed and conducted, following which a national strategy on financial education will be developed and implemented. The Central Bank of Seychelles in collaboration with the Financial Services Authority has been tasked with the mandate for financial literacy in Seychelles. Against this backdrop, the financial literacy baseline survey was commissioned to FinMark Trust, an independent trust based in South Africa. FinMark Trust has focused its efforts on making financial markets work for the poor by facilitating and catalysing development around access to financial services. Much of the work of FinMark Trust is focused on supporting financial inclusion and financial education. 1 The financial literacy baseline survey is the first of its kind to be conducted in Seychelles and its importance needs to be emphasised. The aim of the study was to gauge the level of financial literacy of the population and provide an assessment of the needs of the population including the identification of possible target groups. Assessing the levels of financial literacy in the population is a key component of a successful national strategy for financial education which enables policy makers to identify gaps and design appropriate responses. The results of the survey which are about to be discussed this morning, provides us with a set of data which reflects how the public are making financial decisions vis-a- vis saving, borrowing, budgeting, spending and planning for their financial future in general, amongst other factors. Accordingly, the statistics collected will guide and inform the development of the national strategy on financial education. The collected data which also provides a description of levels of financial literacy in terms of socio- demographic groups will enable policy makers to identify the needs of the population and areas where interventions and attention are most required. In addition, the information collected provides the possibility to conduct repeat surveys to identify change over time. The Central Bank of Seychelles and the Financial Services Authority will be working in collaboration with the public and private stakeholders to achieve the development and implementation of the national strategy. In fact, the procurement for consultancy services to assist with the development of the strategy is currently being initiated. Ladies and gentlemen, these initiatives and engagements towards financial consumer empowerment echo the recent global tempos in respect of financial education. There has been an increased focus on financial literacy internationally, particularly since the 2008 financial crisis which has exposed the effects of lack of financial education amongst consumers, leading many countries to develop or start developing national financial education strategies. Whilst other countries are yet to roll out strategies at the national level, ample efforts are being put into designing financial education programmes or interventions for specific groups of the population. The message is clear: 2 Financial education matters and it matters at many levels. Primarily, from a social welfare perspective, it matters in terms of the ability of people to manage their financial affairs prudently and live within their means. Financial education is meant to empower individuals in the financial marketplace, in terms of increasing their ability to make informed decisions and meaningful participation in the markets, allowing them to better manage personal and household finances and resources. Financially savvy consumers who interact effectively with providers of financial services are more likely to achieve their financial goals and therefore improve their households welfare. Moreover, financial education is instrumental in supporting financial inclusion policies through creation of awareness of the availability of financial products and services and through developing confidence in the use of such products and services. Accordingly, financial education contributes to the development of financial systems and markets as well as to the promotion of more transparent competition amongst financial service providers. In fact, financial education is very much considered as the first line of defence and protection for consumers of financial products and services, since it complements the regulatory and supervisory measures in place. It is widely recognised that individuals across the globe, living in different economic, financial and social circumstances have to take more responsibility for their future financial well-being and protection. It is important to consider that while Authorities will devote resources and work towards establishing mechanisms that will support financial consumer empowerment, it is important to acknowledge that the ultimate responsibility rests with the individual to ensure that financial knowledge and skills acquired are transformed into positive financial behaviour. Ladies and gentlemen, allow me to stress that CBS and its partners remain committed to the development of the financial sector in line with our respective mandates. The successful development of the financial sector must be sustained, amongst other factors, by appropriate legislative and supervisory frameworks, including an effective regulatory framework for financial consumer protection, as recommended in the Financial Sector Development Plan. Accordingly, to further consolidate financial consumer empowerment, CBS and the FSA are working on the development of a legislative framework for financial consumer protection. 3 The proposed framework, which is at a preliminary drafting stage, is specifically aimed at protecting the interests of financial consumers and to fairly, reasonably, and effectively handle financial consumer disputes, thereby reinforcing the confidence of financial consumers in financial markets and promoting their sound development. Such will complement the development of the national strategy on financial education. Ladies and gentlemen, please allow me to conclude my remarks with a few words of acknowledgement. The conduct of the financial literacy baseline survey has been made possible due to the commitment of our faithful partners. May I acknowledge the role of government through the Cabinet of Ministers for approving that such an initiative be conducted. I wish to particularly thank the Financial Services Authority for its involvement throughout the entire process and the National Bureau of Statistics which assisted with the development of the sample for the survey. May I also acknowledge our international partners which are contributing to the funding of these projects, specifically the Investment Climate Facility for Africa and the African Development Bank. The Central Bank also extends its appreciation to Fin Mark Trust for the work conducted. I express my gratitude also to the Central Bank team for making sure the work program moved along smoothly and attained its objectives. Last but not least, I wish to thank the general public for making the time available to participate in the survey. With these remarks, it is my pleasure to invite Mr. Abel Motsomi of FinMark Trust to deliver his presentation on the results of the financial literacy baseline survey. Thank you. 4
